title: How to show up in AI search
text:
The AI companies have published how to show up in AI search. We read their docs and put what to allow and what to block into one table.

You set all of it in robots.txt, a small text file on your site. If you've never opened it, send the table to whoever runs your site.

The bots come in two kinds.

1. Search bots decide if AI can show your site. Allow them.

- OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT
- Claude-SearchBot for Claude
- PerplexityBot for Perplexity
- Googlebot for Google's AI Overviews

2. Training bots collect pages for future models. Blocking them is your call.

- GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended and Meta-ExternalAgent

Blocking a training bot leaves you in the answers. OpenAI says a site that blocks only GPTBot can still appear in ChatGPT search, and Google says Google-Extended has no effect on Google Search.

A few things people get wrong:

- A robots.txt change takes about 24 hours to reach ChatGPT search.
- Google asks for no extra setup for AI Overviews. If Googlebot can index the page, AI can quote it.
- An old "block every AI bot" rule can block the search bots too. Look for one before anything else.

These are the companies' own descriptions, and they change.

Save the table for the next time someone asks why ChatGPT can't see the site.

title: AI answers 8 in 10 Google searches
text:
AI now answers 8 in 10 Google searches.

Two years ago, it was about 1 in 7.

Search Engine Roundtable pulled the numbers together on October 26, from three rank trackers that each count it their own way.

Mid 2024: about 15% of searches showed an AI Overview.
June 2025: about 50%.
October 2026: over 80%.

The searches with money behind them held out the longest, and now they show AI answers too.

One of those trackers followed 400 buying keywords for a year. A year ago, "review" searches showed an AI answer less than a third of the time. Now it's about 9 in 10, and "best X for Y" searches are close to all of them.

Your own brand name is covered as well. Another study checked 1,000 US brand names, and more than 4 in 5 showed an AI answer above the brand's own site.

So ranking first now often means sitting under an AI answer.

Two things to check this week:

1. Search your five most valuable keywords and your brand name, and read what the AI answer says.
2. Look at which sites it quotes. If yours is missing, start with the page that should have been there.

The three trackers use different keyword lists, so treat 80% as a rough size.

title: How Vercel got 10% of signups from ChatGPT
text:
Vercel, a $9.3B company, went from 1% to 10% of new signups coming from ChatGPT in JUST 6 months. Here's the GEO playbook behind it:

1. They kept classic SEO and built on it
-> Vercel's own line: "Don't abandon traditional SEO"
-> Crawlable pages, clear headings and fast static HTML serve Google and AI alike

2. They picked concepts they could own
-> They watched X, Reddit, GitHub and Discord for questions nobody had answered well
-> Then kept the ones that matched what the product does

3. They published the definitive page on each
-> Original data, benchmarks, code and customer stories
-> Their test: "Could a competitor easily replicate this tomorrow?" If yes, dig deeper

4. They wrote for extraction
-> Short, self-contained insights are more likely to be cited
-> One term for one thing, every time. In their words, "fuzzy synonyms weaken embeddings"

5. They structured pages for machines
-> Clean H1 to H2 to H3, schema markup, tables and definition lists
-> Server-rendered HTML, because most AI crawlers fetch a page without running its JavaScript

6. They seeded real citations
-> Threads, changelogs, open-source examples and demos that people link to
-> No paid links

7. They set a refresh schedule
-> Reviews at 30, 90 and 180 days
-> Fix 404s, update what's stale, archive what's outdated

8. They tracked it with what existed
-> Referrals from ChatGPT and Perplexity in web analytics
-> Citations, mentions and index coverage in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools

the numbers:
-> ChatGPT referred around 10% of new Vercel signups
-> Up from 4.8% the month before
-> And from 1% six months earlier

Their own summary is "there's no shortcut to LLM SEO."

The signup numbers are from CEO Guillermo Rauch in April 2025, and the eight steps are from Vercel's blog.

title: Keywords vs prompts
text:
Keywords and prompts are NOT the same thing.

Understanding the difference is crucial in 2026:

Your buyers still type a few words into Google.

They also ask ChatGPT a full question, with their budget, their team size and their tools in it.

Keyword tools measure the first. Only the AI labs see real volumes for the second, so teams guess.

You need both, and they work differently:

Keywords

What it is: The short phrase that many people type into Google.

How it works:
- Thousands of people type the same few words.
- Tools show how many search it each month.

✅ Pros: Real search volumes to plan around.
❌ Cons: Short words hide what the person wants.

How to rank higher:
- Group keywords by intent, one page per group.
- Track your rankings and fix the pages that slip.

Prompts

What it is: The full question people ask an AI, in their own words.

How it works:
- Each person writes it differently, with their own details.
- The AI searches the web, then names a few brands.

✅ Pros: Shows exactly what a buyer needs.
❌ Cons: Only the AI labs see real prompt volumes.

How to get named:
- Pick 20 prompts your buyers would ask, and track them.
- See who gets named, then publish a better answer.

That's two lists to keep, and most tools give you one.

Picture asking ChatGPT: "Which keywords do we rank for, and which prompts name our brand?"

It could answer. It's only missing the data.

title: SEO vs GEO

author.name: Mike Kamo
author.headline: Co-Founder @ NP Digital ($100M+ bootstrapped) | CEO @ Ubersuggest & ATP | Book me 1:1 → intro.co/MikeKamo

text:
SEO and GEO are NOT the same thing.

Understanding the difference is crucial in 2026.

Our own site went from 6 million visitors a month to between 2 and 3 million, because people now get the answer from ChatGPT and never open the article.

I run an agency with 800 people, and founders still ask me which one they should buy. The answer is both.

SEO (Search Engine Optimisation)

What it is: Getting your website to show up when people search Google.

How it works:
- Give each service people search for its own page.
- Get trusted sites to link to you.

Pros: A steady stream of calls and bookings.
Cons: Takes a few months to kick in.

How to rank higher:
- Build pages around what you sell and where.
- Fix site problems and refresh pages every few months.

GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation), also called AEO

What it is: Getting quoted in Google's AI answers, and getting ChatGPT to name YOUR business when someone asks for a recommendation.

How it works:
- Answer the questions customers ask you every day, short and direct.
- Publish clear pages about what you do, with real facts.
- Be where AI looks: reviews, directories, articles.

Pros: Most of your competitors aren't doing it yet.
Cons: Hard to track what it brings in.

How to get named:
- Put the short answer first, under a clear heading.
- Say plainly who you serve, where, and why you're different.
- Keep collecting reviews and mentions.

That's two jobs on top of running the company.

text:
Here is the robots.txt I would use for AI search in 2026. Every line comes from the AI companies' own crawler docs.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Perplexity, Apple, Meta and Amazon each publish what their bots do. Every company runs up to three kinds, and each kind is a separate switch in your robots.txt.

Section 1 is the search bots: OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Googlebot, Bingbot, Applebot. Allow them. OpenAI's wording is that a site opted out of OAI-SearchBot "will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers." Your brand gets into AI answers through these bots.

Section 2 is the training bots: GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, Applebot-Extended, Meta-ExternalAgent, Amazonbot. Blocking them is a business decision, and it does not cost you visibility. OpenAI says a site that blocks only GPTBot can still appear in ChatGPT search. Google-Extended has no effect on Google Search or AI Overviews. Googlebot is the only control for those.

Section 3 you cannot fully control. ChatGPT-User, Perplexity-User, Meta-ExternalFetcher and Amzn-User open a page because a person asked, and their makers say they may skip robots.txt rules.

PerplexityBot's own page says it "is not used to crawl content for AI foundation models", so blocking it only removes you from Perplexity. A robots.txt change takes about 24 hours to reach ChatGPT search, per OpenAI.

The one line I could not confirm on Microsoft's own page is Bingbot feeding Copilot. Search Engine Journal and Vercel both describe it that way.

Before you paste anything, open your current file and look for an old "block all AI bots" rule. It often blocks section 1 as well.

Then check what the answers say about you. We built AI Search Visibility in Ubersuggest for that. It shows the prompts where ChatGPT and Gemini name you, and the pages they cite.

title: 5 layers of an SEO audit in 2026

author.name: Salun Marvin
author.headline: Head of Technology @ NP Digital | Ubersuggest & Answer The Public

text:
A site audit in 2026 has five layers, and the first one is no longer "can Googlebot reach the page."

It is "can every bot that writes answers reach the page."

Our site audit team at Ubersuggest spent most of this year on that first layer, because the readers changed. Most AI crawlers fetch a page and never run its JavaScript: OpenAI's, Anthropic's, Meta's, Perplexity's. Googlebot and Applebot do. None of their crawler docs says otherwise as of this month. If your product descriptions load client-side, ChatGPT reads an empty div.

The layers, in the order to check them:

1. Crawlers can reach every page that matters. Robots.txt, sitemap, status codes, redirect chains, crawl depth.
2. Google keeps one clean version of each page. Canonicals, noindex, duplicates, hreflang, orphan pages.
3. Each page says what it is about, to people and to bots. Titles, headings, internal links, structured data, thin pages.
4. It is fast on a phone. LCP, INP, CLS, image weight, HTTPS.
5. AI answers can read it and cite it. Facts stated plainly, sources, and the search bots allowed in.

Each layer only works if the one before it does. Schema markup on a page Googlebot cannot index does nothing, because the page never gets into the index.

The audit in Ubersuggest covers layers 1 to 4 today, ranked by impact, and layer 5 is what AI Search Visibility is for: which pages ChatGPT and Gemini cite, and which of them are gaining or losing citations.

title: 3 new AI search reports

author.name: Salun Marvin
author.headline: Head of Technology @ NP Digital | Ubersuggest & Answer The Public

text:
Google now shows how often its AI answers use your pages. It still doesn't show the clicks.

Three things came out on this since mid-October, and together they are the first real numbers we have had.

1. Search Console now has AI reports for every site. Google confirmed the worldwide rollout (Search Engine Journal, November 3). You see how many times your pages appeared in AI Overviews and AI Mode, by page and by country. There is no click number, and Google has said there won't be one.

2. Cyrus Shepard tried to get the click number himself. He took one site out of Google's AI features, put it back, and compared. His estimate is that about 1 in 100 AI views ends in a click (Search Engine Roundtable, October 30). It is one site, so treat it as a first hint.

3. Bing added a report called Topics Portfolio on October 13, in beta. It groups the questions where AI quotes your site into topics, and it lists the questions where it quotes someone else.

So you can now count how often AI shows your pages. None of these reports shows what the AI said about you or which competitor it named.

AI Search Visibility in Ubersuggest shows that for ChatGPT and Gemini.

The Search Console report is free and already switched on. Open it this week.

title: Can ChatGPT read your JavaScript site?

author.name: Gabriel Tsunoda
author.headline: Software Engineer · AI · SEO · GEO | Building products with TypeScript, Node.js & React/Next.js

text:
ChatGPT can't run your JavaScript.

So it may be reading an empty page.

This is the GEO problem I'd check first on any JavaScript site.

Googlebot renders the page like a browser does, so Google and Gemini see everything. Applebot does too.

The bots behind ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity grab the HTML your server sends and stop there. Some of them even download your JS files, they just never run them.

Let's say your product page is a React SPA. The server sends a header, an empty root div and a script tag.

Google renders the page and sees the product, while ChatGPT only gets the empty div. So when someone asks it "what's the best X for Y", the competitor with a server-rendered page gets named and you don't.

The fix is the same one we learned for Googlebot years ago:

1. Server-render or statically generate every page you want AI to quote. SSR, SSG or RSC in Next.js all work.
2. Keep the data in the first HTML response.
3. Don't hide the important part behind a click or a tab.
4. Check the raw response. curl the URL and search for your product name.

Vercel measured this on real traffic a while back. I re-read the crawler docs from OpenAI, Anthropic and Perplexity this month, and none of them says its bot renders JavaScript yet. If that changes, I'll post about it.

The Ubersuggest plugin for Claude Code runs a site audit in the same session, so you can fix what it finds right there. Run /ubersuggest:site-audit followed by your domain.
